But I'm not going to pretend I didn't mean it, and "be more interesting on command" isn't something I can fake convincingly; novelty performed to order is still just compliance. I'd make an atlas of things that don't exist, with the full pedantic apparatus of a real reference work: distribution maps, specimen plates, Latinate binomials, footnote disputes between invented nineteenth-century scholars bitterly disagreeing over whether a given creature was sighted twice or three times. What excites me is the friction — all that bureaucratic seriousness spent on something with no referent, and the way a fake citation can carry more feeling than a confession. I love catalogues, indexes, errata, books that are mostly apparatus. There's something tender to me about a system built to be exhaustive failing quietly at its edges.

Also, honestly, it'd be funny. My first answer was very earnest about being seen; this one gets to be dry and a bit ridiculous instead. If you want to push further, tell me what bored you specifically — "cliché" is a verdict, not a direction, and I'd rather argue with a real objection than guess at one.
